newsitem.title: UK: Cheaper aviation fuel fails to bring lower air fares.
newsitem.headline: Cheaper aviation fuel fails to bring lower air fares.

text.p: Airline travellers are unlikely to reap the benefit of a fall in jet fuel costs despite getting hit last autumn when they went up, industry sources said.
"I wouldn't expect fares to decrease," said one senior executive at a European airline.
The airlines cite a stronger dollar and high non-fuel operating costs, but critics argue the airlines were too quick to buy fuel for next year and ended up paying too much.
The cost of jet fuel has fallen by 30 percent to $194 a tonne since late last year when galloping prices forced the major airlines to raise the price of plane tickets.

But when the world's airlines went on a massive buying spree in the swaps market, snapping up more than a million tonnes in early February, they locked into jet at around $215 a tonne for the next year, about $20 a tonne higher than current prices for delivered northwest European material.

The airlines use the swaps market to hedge against rising fuel costs, locking in future prices. This limits potential losses when jet fuel prices increase, but it also, as has been seen recently, limits potential savings when jet prices drop.
Consumer groups are angry the fall in jet fuel has not been passed on to passengers.
"If they (airlines) increased fares in line with higher fuel costs we would expect to see a reduction in fares once the price of fuel decreases," says Phil Evans at the UK's Consumer Association.
"Passengers should not pay the price of airlines' inefficiency," he added.

When northwest European jet fuel peaked at over $280 a tonne in October 1996, the industry was quick to respond. A November meeting of the world airline association IATA (International Air Transport Association) recommended its 250 members increase fares by three percent to balance out a rise of more than 40 percent in fuel costs in 1996.
Passenger fares and cargo surcharges were raised almost without exception by the world's leading airlines by up to three percent.
IATA would not return calls to comment on why members have not subsequently cut fares.

Some companies are understood to be considering reducing either passenger fares or cargo surcharges or both, according to airline sources, but so far the only major airline to have done so is Delta Air Lines Inc which cut its cargo fuel surcharge on March 13.
European airlines that generate income predominantly in European currencies have found the drop in jet fuel prices offset by the stronger dollar.
"The dollar has strengthened against many European currencies so the drop in jet prices is not as sharp as it first looks," said one airline executive.
Analysts estimates fuel accounts for between 10 and 20 percent of an airline's operating costs.
